pages.title: Getting started
pages.summary: From the demo or your first sign-in to adding, scheduling and completing your first task, in about five minutes.
pages.html:
Getting started

This guide takes you from opening OpenTodo for the first time to adding a task, giving it a date and ticking it off. It takes about five minutes. You can follow along in the demo or on your own server.

Open OpenTodo#

You have three ways in.

Try the demo#

Go to opentodo-demo.pixari.dev and select Try the demo. You get a private sandbox filled with sample projects and tasks. Nobody else can see it, and it is deleted after two hours without activity (and every night), so don't keep anything personal there.

Set up your own server#

The first person to open a new OpenTodo server creates the owner account. Enter your name, email and a password of at least 10 characters, then select Create owner account. After that, sign-up is closed: other people join with an invitation from you (see Sharing and comments).

Join with an invitation#

Open the invitation link you were sent, choose a name and password, and you're in. If your server offers single sign-on or passkeys, the sign-in screen shows those buttons too.

Once you're signed in, the app is stored on your device. You can keep using it without a connection, and it catches up with the server when you're back online.

Find your way around#

The sidebar on the left lists your views and projects. On a phone it's behind the menu button at the top left.

  • Inbox collects tasks that don't belong to a project yet.
  • Today shows what's due today, with anything overdue at the top.
  • Upcoming shows the days ahead, grouped by date.
  • Projects are your own lists, like "Home renovation" or "Work".

The circle to the left of each task completes it. The small line under the title shows the date, labels and project. More on all the views in Views.

Add your first task#

  1. Press q, or click the Add a task box at the top of the list.
  2. Type what you need to do, for example Call the dentist.
  3. Press Enter.

The task appears straight away. The box stays open, so you can type the next one right after.

Where the task goes depends on where you are: in a project it goes into that project, in Today it's due today, and in the Inbox it waits there until you sort it.

Give it a date#

You can schedule a task while you type it. Quick add understands everyday words:

Call the dentist tomorrow at 9am

As you type, small chips appear under the box to show what OpenTodo understood: a date chip for "tomorrow at 9am", and below them the title that will be saved. If a word was picked up by mistake ("May" as in the name, not the month), click the × on its chip and it stays part of the title.

The same line can also set a project with #, a label with @, a priority from p1 (highest) to p4, and how long it will take with +, like +15m. The quick add reference lists everything it understands, in six languages.

To change the date later, open the task (click it, or select it and press Enter) and use Due in the panel that opens.

Complete it#

When you're done, click the circle next to the task, or select it with j and k and press c. The task leaves the list and moves to Completed in the sidebar. Changed your mind? Open Completed and reopen it.

Get it on your phone#

OpenTodo runs in the browser, and you can install it like an app on your phone, tablet or computer. It then opens in its own window and works offline. See Installing the app.

Help inside the app#

Every guide on this site is also in the app: select Help at the bottom of the sidebar, or press g then ?. It works offline and matches the version of your server. Many screens have a small Help link that opens the right section next to what you're doing, without closing it.

Where to go next#

  • Tasks and projects: notes, subtasks, priorities and organising your work.
  • Views: Today, Upcoming, the calendar and views you save yourself.
  • Recurring tasks and reminders: repeat a task every week and get a nudge on time.
  • Keyboard shortcuts: press ? in the app to see them all.

pages.title: Installing the app
pages.summary: Put OpenTodo on your home screen or desktop so it opens in its own window and works offline, on iPhone, Android, Windows, macOS and Linux.
pages.html:
Installing the app

OpenTodo is a web app you can install. Once installed it has its own icon, opens in its own window without browser bars, starts without a connection, and on most platforms can show reminders while it's closed. There is no app store involved: you install it from your server's address, and updates arrive by themselves.

Before you start, open your OpenTodo address in the browser and sign in once. Installing needs a secure address (one starting with https://); if your browser offers no install option at all, ask whoever runs your server to set that up.

iPhone and iPad#

  1. Open your OpenTodo address in Safari.
  2. Tap the Share button (the square with an arrow pointing up).
  3. Scroll down and tap Add to Home Screen, then Add.

OpenTodo now has an icon on your home screen. Open it from there from now on. On iOS 16.4 and later, push notifications for reminders work only in the installed app, not in a Safari tab; turn them on in Settings → Notifications inside the app. See Notifications.

Recent iOS versions also offer Add to Home Screen from the share menu of other browsers. If you don't see it, use Safari.

Android#

  1. Open your OpenTodo address in Chrome (Edge and Samsung Internet work the same way).
  2. Open the browser menu (⋮).
  3. Tap Install app. On some versions it's called Add to Home screen.

Chrome sometimes shows an install banner at the bottom of the screen on its own; tapping it does the same thing.

After installing, OpenTodo also appears in Android's share menu, so you can send a link or some text from another app straight into a new task. See Capturing pages.

Windows, macOS, Linux and ChromeOS#

In Chrome or Edge:

  1. Open your OpenTodo address.
  2. Click the install icon at the right end of the address bar (a small screen with a down arrow), or open the browser menu and choose Install OpenTodo (in Edge: Apps → Install this site as an app).
  3. Confirm with Install.

OpenTodo opens in its own window and gets an entry in your Start menu, Dock or app launcher. You can pin it to the taskbar like any other app.

In Safari on macOS (Sonoma or later), choose File → Add to Dock.

Firefox on the desktop doesn't install web apps. You can still use OpenTodo in a Firefox tab with everything working, including offline use once the page has loaded.

Keep using it offline#

The installed app keeps a full copy of your tasks on the device. You can open it on a plane, add and complete tasks, and it syncs when you're online again. The status at the top right tells you where things stand. More in Offline and sync.

Updates#

When your server is updated, the app fetches the new version in the background and switches to it on its own, usually with one quick reload. If you think you're still on an old version, close the app completely and open it again.

Remove it#

Remove it the way you remove any app on that device: long-press the icon and choose Remove App (iPhone) or Uninstall (Android), or use Uninstall from the app window's menu on a computer. Your tasks stay on your server.

Signing out (Settings → Session → Sign out) clears the copy of your tasks on that device. Changes that haven't reached the server yet are uploaded first when you're online.

pages.title: Tasks and projects
pages.summary: Add and edit tasks, write notes, break work into subtasks, set priorities and organise everything into projects and sub-projects.
pages.html:
Tasks and projects

A task is one thing to do. A project is a list of tasks that belong together. This guide covers both, from adding a task to arranging projects inside each other.

Add a task#

Press q anywhere in a task list, type, and press Enter. The box stays focused so you can add several in a row.

You can fill in details as you type:

Order new taps friday #Home @errand p2 +20m

This creates "Order new taps", due Friday, in the project Home, with the label errand, priority 2 and an estimate of 20 minutes. Chips under the box show what was understood before you press Enter. The quick add reference has every word and symbol it knows.

New tasks without a project land in the Inbox. Tasks added inside a project go into that project, and tasks added in Today are due today.

Edit a task#

Click a task, or select it with j / k and press Enter, to open its panel. Every change is saved as you make it; there is no Save button.

In the panel you can change:

  • Title and Notes. Notes can have headings, bold and italic text, links, and bullet, numbered and check lists.
  • Project, Section and Parent task, to move it somewhere else.
  • Priority, from P1 (most important) to P4 (the default).
  • Due, a date with an optional time.
  • Reminders, Estimate and Repeat. See Recurring tasks and reminders and Time blocking.
  • Labels, Subtasks and, further down, Comments and History.

Close the panel with Esc or the × at the top. On a phone the panel covers the list; close it to go back.

Quick changes from the list#

You don't have to open a task to change it. Select it and press:

Key Does
1 to 4 Set the priority
c Complete or reopen
L Add labels (type to search, Enter to add or create)
e Set the estimate (20, 45m, 1h30)
s Schedule it on the Day calendar
Delete Move it to the Trash

Write notes#

The notes field formats as you type. Start a line with - for a bullet list, 1. for a numbered list, [ ] for a checklist or # for a heading. Select text and press Ctrl+B for bold or Ctrl+K for a link (⌘ on a Mac). If two of your devices edit the same note at the same time, both sets of changes are kept.

Dates and times#

A due date is just a calendar day, and a time is the time on the clock where you are. A task due Tuesday at 09:00 shows Tuesday at 09:00 on every device, even when you travel.

For things that happen at a fixed moment, like a call with someone in another country, tick Fixed to time zone under Due (or press z with the panel open). The task is then tied to your current time zone, and devices elsewhere show it converted to their local time, with the original time as a hint.

Complete, reopen and delete#

Click the circle next to a task, or press c. Completed tasks move to Completed in the sidebar, where you can reopen them.

Deleting a task (the Delete button in the panel, or Delete in the list) moves it to the Trash, along with its subtasks. You can restore it from there. See Trash and history.

Break a task into subtasks#

Big tasks are easier as a few small steps. To add one:

  • open the task and type in Add subtask, or
  • select the task in the list and press a.

Subtasks appear indented under their parent, and the parent shows your progress, like 1/3. You can nest subtasks inside subtasks.

To turn an existing task into a subtask, select it and press Tab: it moves under the task above it. Shift+Tab moves it back out. You can also pick a Parent task in the panel. Use ← and → to fold and unfold a parent's subtasks.

Completing a parent completes all its open subtasks too. When you tick off the last open subtask, OpenTodo asks whether to complete the parent as well; press Enter for yes.

Organise with projects#

Projects keep related tasks together. To create one, click + next to Projects in the sidebar, type a name and choose Create. Pick a parent project in the same form to make it a sub-project.

The Project menu at the top right of a project lets you:

  • pick a color,
  • Move to another project, or back to the top level (shortcut m),
  • Rename it,
  • Archive it, which hides it and its sub-projects from the sidebar while keeping every task,
  • Delete project, which moves it to the Trash.

The number next to each project in the sidebar counts its open tasks. When a project with sub-projects is folded, the number includes them.

Inside a project you can also group tasks into sections and show them as a board. That has its own guide: Sections and boards.

Sub-projects#

Sub-projects work like folders: "Work" can hold "Q4 launch", which can hold more. A project's page lists its sub-projects at the bottom with their task counts. Use the small arrow next to a project in the sidebar, or ← / →, to fold and unfold it. Folding is remembered on each device separately.

When a project is done#

When you complete the last open task of a project, OpenTodo offers to archive it; press Enter to accept or any other key to keep it. Projects that have had no open tasks for 30 days are archived automatically, with a notice you can undo. You can turn that off in Settings → Projects (each device has its own setting). To bring an archived project back, open Settings → Projects and select Restore next to it under Archived projects; see Trash and history.

Put things in order#

In the Inbox and in projects, you decide the order. Drag a task to a new place (on a touch screen, press and hold first), or select it and press Alt+↑ / Alt+↓. Alt+Shift+↑ sends it to the top. Dropping a task on the middle of another one makes it a subtask. Projects in the sidebar can be reordered the same way.

Today, Upcoming, labels and filters sort themselves by date and priority, so dragging is switched off there.

Tips#

  • Keep the Inbox as a landing spot: capture fast, then sort into projects once a day.
  • Use priorities sparingly. If everything is P1, nothing is.
  • A task with an estimate shows it on the row, like 30m, which makes it easy to spot quick wins. The Quick wins button above most lists shows only tasks of 15 minutes or less.

pages.title: Views
pages.summary: Inbox, Today, Upcoming, Assigned to me, Completed and the calendar, plus views you save yourself, dashboards and the view each device opens on.
pages.html:
Views

A view is a way of looking at your tasks. OpenTodo comes with a handful, and you can save your own. Every view is built from the copy of your tasks on your device, so they all work offline and update the moment something changes.

The built-in views#

They're at the top of the sidebar. Each has a shortcut: press g, then the letter.

View Shows Shortcut
Inbox Tasks that aren't in a project yet g i
Today Tasks due today, with overdue ones first g t
Upcoming Tasks due after today, grouped by day g u
Assigned to me Open tasks assigned to you, across projects g a
Day and Week Your timed tasks on a calendar g d, g w
Completed What you finished most recently g c
Filter Any search you can describe g f
Trash Deleted tasks and projects g x
Activity What changed in your shared projects g h

The numbers next to the names count open tasks.

Plan your day with Today#

Today is where most people start. Overdue tasks sit in their own group at the top, in red, so nothing slips. Below them are today's tasks, sorted by time.

Anything you add here with quick add is due today, unless you type another date. To push a task to later, open it and change Due, or press s to place it on the Day calendar.

Plan your week with Upcoming#

Upcoming lists everything that has a date after today, under headings like Tomorrow and the weekday names. It's a good place for a short weekly review: scan the next few days, move what won't fit, and spot empty days.

When you want to see the hours, switch to Week, which shows your timed tasks as blocks on a grid. See Time blocking.

Narrow a list by duration#

Above most lists are four buttons: Quick wins (15 minutes or less), Under 30 min, Over 1 h and Unestimated. Turn one on to see only matching tasks; select it again to clear it. Your choice is remembered on that device. Estimates are set with e or in the task panel.

Save your own views#

When the built-in views aren't enough, describe what you want in the Filter view, then save it. For example, @waiting & open lists everything you're waiting on, and due <= 7 days & p1 shows urgent tasks for the coming week. The filter language is explained in Labels and filters.

To save the current filter, press s in the results (or use the save button), and give it a name. Saved views are pinned to the Views group in the sidebar with a live count, and they sync to all your devices.

Each saved view can group its tasks (by project, date, priority or label) and sort them (by date, priority, your own order, creation time or title). Change these from the top of the view. To change the query itself, press /, edit it and press Enter.

The All link next to Views (or g v) opens the list of all your saved views. From there you can rename, reorder, unpin or delete them.

Build a dashboard#

A dashboard puts up to six saved views side by side, each showing its count and first ten tasks. It's handy for a morning review: "Due this week", "Deep work" and "Waiting on others" on one screen.

Open the views list (g v), choose + New dashboard, name it, then add saved views as panels from the dashboard's header. On a phone the panels stack. Move between panels with Tab, and through a panel's tasks with j / k.

Choose where the app opens#

Each device can open on a different view: your laptop on a "Work" view, your phone on Today. Pick it in Settings → Start view, or from a saved view's menu with Set as start view on this device. If that view is deleted later, the device opens on the Inbox and tells you why.

Tips#

  • Subtasks show up on their own in Today and Upcoming, with their parent's name next to them, so you see exactly what's due.
  • Views that sort by date (Today, Upcoming, labels, filters) can't be reordered by hand. Projects and the Inbox can.
  • Filter queries has ten ready-made examples to copy.

pages.title: Sections and boards
pages.summary: Split a project into stages with sections, and switch it to a board to move cards between columns by drag or keyboard.

toc.text: Rename, reorder or delete a section
Get around the board with the keyboard

pages.html:
Sections and boards

Sections divide a project into parts, like "Planning", "In progress" and "Waiting", or "Kitchen", "Bathroom" and "Garden". The same project can be shown as a list with headings or as a board with one column per section.

Add a section#

Open a project and select + Add section at the bottom of the list. Type a name and press Enter. You can add the next one straight away.

Each heading shows how many open tasks it holds. Tasks without a section are listed first under No section.

Add tasks to a section#

Select the + on a section heading and type: the task goes straight into that section. You can also open any task and choose a Section in its panel.

Rename, reorder or delete a section#

Use the ⋯ menu on a section heading:

  • Rename
  • Move it up or down (left or right on the board)
  • Delete section. Its open tasks aren't deleted; they move to No section.

Fold a section with the small arrow next to its name. Folding is remembered on that device only.

Switch to a board#

At the top of the project, choose Board (or press v). Each section becomes a column, with No section first. Press v again, or choose List, to switch back.

The choice is remembered for each project on each device. Your laptop can show "Q4 launch" as a board while your phone shows it as a list. On a narrow screen the board scrolls sideways.

Move cards between columns#

  • Drag a card to another column, or to a place within a column. On a touch screen, press and hold the card first.
  • Keyboard: select a card and press Shift+→ or Shift+←. The card stays selected, so you can keep moving it.
  • Panel: open the task and pick another Section.

Moving with the keyboard or the panel puts the card at the bottom of the new column.

Get around the board with the keyboard#

Key Does
h / l or ← / → Jump to the previous or next column
j / k Move up and down within a column
Shift+← / Shift+→ Move the selected card to the previous or next column
a Add a task to the selected card's column
Enter Open the card

Good to know#

  • Moving a task to another project removes it from its section, because sections belong to one project.
  • If someone deletes a section while you were moving a task into it on another device, the task ends up under No section. Nothing is lost.
  • Sections are part of the export and come back when you import it.

Ideas for sections#

  • A simple flow: To do, Doing, Done.
  • By place: Kitchen, Bathroom, Garden for a renovation.
  • By week: This week, Next week, Later for a launch plan.

pages.title: Labels and filters
pages.summary: Tag tasks across projects with labels, then find exactly what you need with the filter language and save it as a view.

toc.text: Add a label to a task
Save a filter as a view

pages.html:
Labels and filters

Projects say where a task belongs. Labels say what kind of task it is, across all projects: @call, @errand, @waiting, @deep-work. Filters then let you ask questions like "every call I need to make this week".

Add a label to a task#

Pick whichever is quickest:

  • Type it in quick add: Phone the bank @call.
  • Select a task and press L, start typing, and press Enter. The picker stays open so you can add more.
  • Open the task and use Labels in the panel.

If the label doesn't exist yet, typing its name and pressing Enter creates it. Labels show as small colored chips on the task. To remove one, open the task and select the × on the chip.

See everything with one label#

The Labels group in the sidebar lists your labels with the number of open tasks for each. Select one to see all its tasks, grouped by project.

All next to Labels (or g l) opens the full list. From there, or from a label's ⋯ menu in the sidebar, you can:

  • Rename it or change its Color. Every task shows the new name immediately.
  • Move up or Move down in the list.
  • Merge into… another label: tasks with the first label get the second one instead, and the first is deleted. Handy when you end up with both "Errand" and "errand".
  • Delete label: it's removed from every task.

If two of your devices created the same label while offline, both copies appear with a duplicate marker and an offer to merge them.

Labels are personal. In a shared project, other members don't see the labels you add.

Find tasks with a filter#

Open Filter in the sidebar (or press g f) and type a query. Results appear as you type, grouped by project.

A query combines small pieces:

Piece Means Example
@name has this label @call
#name in this project #Work
##name in this project or its sub-projects ##Work
p1 … p4 priority p1
today, tomorrow, overdue, no date due then, or not at all overdue
due <= 7 days due within the next week due before friday
search: text words in the title or notes search: invoice
completed include completed tasks #Home & completed

Join them with & (and), | (or) and ! (not), and use brackets to group:

(@call | @errand) & due <= 7 days

That reads: tasks labeled call or errand, due within the next seven days. A few more:

  • #Work & p1 & due <= tomorrow: the most important work for today and tomorrow.
  • overdue & no project: overdue tasks still sitting in the Inbox.
  • @waiting & !#Work: everything you're waiting on, outside work.

Names with spaces go in quotes: #"Client A". Upper and lower case don't matter. If you mistype, a message under the box says where, and the previous results stay visible.

Press Enter to jump from the box to the first result, and Esc to go back. ↑ and ↓ in the box bring back your recent queries.

The full language, with ten worked examples, is in Filter queries.

Save a filter as a view#

When a query is useful, keep it: press s in the results, give it a name, and it appears under Views in the sidebar with a live count. Saved views sync to your other devices. See Views for grouping, sorting and dashboards.

Tips#

  • Labels for context work well: @call, @computer, @errand, @home. Then a view like @errand & due <= 2 days is your shopping list.
  • A @waiting label plus a pinned "Waiting on others" view makes follow-ups hard to forget.
  • Filters run on your device. They're instant, and they work offline.

pages.title: Recurring tasks and reminders
pages.summary: Make a task repeat every week, month or weekday, skip an occurrence, and get reminded at the right moment.

toc.text: Complete, skip or split off one occurrence

pages.html:
Recurring tasks and reminders

Some tasks come back: pay the rent, water the plants, the weekly one-to-one. Make them repeat once and OpenTodo moves them forward each time you complete them. Add a reminder and you'll get a nudge when it matters.

Make a task repeat#

Open the task and type a rule into Repeat, such as every week. A list of suggestions appears as you type. Under the field you'll see the next three dates, so you can check the rule does what you meant.

Rules are set in the task panel. Quick add doesn't read them: typing every monday there doesn't make a task repeat. Add the task first, then open it and set Repeat.

Repeating tasks show a ↻ symbol on the row. To stop repeating, select the × next to the rule.

Rules you can write#

Rule Repeats
every day, every 3 days daily, or every few days
every weekday Monday to Friday
every week, every 2 weeks weekly or fortnightly
every monday, every mon, wed, fri on those weekdays
every month, every 15th monthly, on the same day or a fixed day
every last day, every last friday at the end of the month
every 2nd tuesday the second Tuesday of each month
every year once a year on the same date

Two extras work with any of these:

  • After completion: every 2 weeks after completion counts from the day you actually finish, not from the due date. Good for things like "change the water filter".
  • An end: add until 2026-12-31 or for 10 times to stop the series.

Rules are in English, whichever language you use for dates in quick add. Every detail is in the recurring task rules reference.

Complete, skip or split off one occurrence#

When you complete a repeating task, that occurrence is recorded in Completed, and the task moves to its next date. If it was overdue, it jumps to the next date from today, so missed occurrences don't pile up.

The buttons under the rule handle the exceptions:

  • Skip (Shift+S) moves to the next date without recording a completion. Use it when this week's run is cancelled.
  • This occurrence only (Shift+O) splits the current occurrence off as a normal task you can change freely, while the series moves on. Use it when this week's meeting is on Thursday instead.

Changing the title, notes, project, priority, labels or time of a repeating task changes the whole series.

Add a reminder#

Open a task and select + Add reminder under Reminders. Choose one of:

  • At due time, 10 minutes before, 30 minutes before, 1 hour before or 1 day before,
  • Custom offset…, for any number of minutes, hours or days before or after,
  • At a specific date and time…, for a fixed moment that doesn't depend on the due date.

A task can have several reminders. Reminders relative to the due time move with it: change the due date and they follow, and on a repeating task they carry over to the next occurrence. If the task has a date but no time, "before" and "after" count from 09:00 that day.

When a reminder goes off#

While OpenTodo is open, a reminder pops up in the corner of the screen with Snooze 10 min, 1 hour, Tomorrow 09:00 and Dismiss. This works without a connection and without any permission.

To get reminders when the app is closed, turn on notifications for each device in Settings → Notifications. On an iPhone this needs the installed app. See Notifications.

Snoozing or dismissing on one device applies to all of them.

Shared projects#

Reminders are personal. On a task in a shared project, your reminders are yours alone: other members don't see them and don't get them. You can add reminders even if you can only view the project.

Tips#

  • For bills, use a day-of-month rule (every 1st) plus a 1 day before reminder.
  • A reminder on a task without a time fires at 09:00 for "at due time". Give the task a time if you need it earlier.
  • Deleted tasks don't remind you. If you restore one, its reminders come back.

pages.title: Time blocking
pages.summary: Estimate how long tasks take, then place them on the Day or Week calendar to see whether your plan fits the day.

toc.text: Estimate how long a task takes
Place a task on the calendar

pages.html:
Time blocking

A to-do list tells you what to do. A calendar tells you when. Time blocking puts the two together: give tasks an estimate, drop them on the Day or Week calendar, and you can see at a glance whether your day is realistic.

Estimate how long a task takes#

Select a task and press e, then type 20, 45m, 1h or 1h30 and press Enter. In the task panel, Estimate also has buttons for 15 minutes up to 2 hours. In quick add, write +30m or +1h30.

The estimate shows on the task row, like 45m or 1h 30m.

Open the calendar#

Choose Day or Week in the sidebar, or press g d or g w.

  • Tasks with a date and a time appear as blocks at that time. The block is as tall as the estimate.
  • A timed task without an estimate gets a 30-minute block with a dashed outline.
  • Tasks with a date but no time wait in the Unscheduled lane at the top of their day.
  • A red line marks the current time.

Use ‹ and › (or [ and ]) to go back and forward, and Today (or t) to come back.

Place a task on the calendar#

Drag a task from the Unscheduled lane onto a time slot. Its due date and time become that slot. The grid works in 15-minute steps.

To plan from your lists, open the side list with Plan from a list and drag tasks from there onto the calendar.

To change how long something takes, drag the bottom edge of its block. Dropping a block back on the Unscheduled lane keeps the date and removes the time.

With the keyboard#

Every move works without a mouse.

  1. In Today, a project or any list, select a task and press s. The Day view opens with the task ready to place.
  2. Move it with the arrow keys: ↑ / ↓ by 15 minutes, ← / → by a day.
  3. Press Enter to place it, or Esc to cancel.

On the calendar itself, j / k select tasks, the arrows move the selected one, Shift+↑ / Shift+↓ shorten or lengthen it, and u takes it off the grid while keeping its date.

See whether the day fits#

Each day's header adds up the estimates of its open tasks and compares them with your day length, for example 4h 15m / 8h. When you've planned more than the day holds, the header is marked as over capacity. That's your cue to move something.

Tasks that overlap in time are shown side by side, with a marker, so nothing hides behind something else.

Completing a task removes its block and lowers the day's total.

Adjust the grid#

In Settings → Calendar you can set when the grid starts and ends (6:00 to 22:00 by default; you can still scroll beyond) and how long your working day is (8 hours by default). These settings belong to each device, so your phone and laptop can differ.

Tips#

  • Estimate generously at first. After a week you'll know how long "quick" things really take.
  • Leave gaps. A day planned to the minute falls apart at the first phone call.
  • The Quick wins button above your lists shows tasks of 15 minutes or less, good for filling a short gap.
  • Dates and times you set on the calendar are ordinary due dates, so they show up in Today and Upcoming as well, and in calendar apps connected over CalDAV.

pages.title: Sharing and comments
pages.summary: Share a project with people on your server, choose what they can do, assign tasks, and talk it through in comments with @mentions.

toc.text: Leave or hand over a project

pages.html:
Sharing and comments

Projects can be shared with other people who have an account on the same OpenTodo server: your partner for the house move, your team for a launch. Everyone sees the same tasks, edits sync to everyone within seconds, and each task has a comment thread.

Share a project#

  1. Open the project and select Share at the top (or press Shift+S).
  2. Type the person's email address.
  3. Pick a role and select Share.

The project appears on their devices the next time they sync, with all its tasks. Shared projects have a small people icon in the sidebar.

You can only add people who already have an account on your server. If they don't, invite them first (see below).

Choose a role#

Role Can
viewer see the project and its tasks, and comment
editor also add, edit, complete and delete tasks, and assign them
admin also rename, recolor and archive the project, and manage members
owner everything, including deleting the project and handing it over

Every project has exactly one owner. To change someone's role, open Share and pick a new one next to their name. Remove takes them out of the project.

For viewers, the project is read-only: the add box and edit controls are switched off, with a note saying so.

Invite someone new#

Sign-up on an OpenTodo server is closed by default, so new people join with an invitation. If you're the owner or an admin of the server, go to Settings → Members, optionally enter their email, choose how long the link stays valid, and select Create invitation. Copy the link and send it to them however you like; OpenTodo doesn't send emails. The link works once.

If you're not an admin of the server, ask whoever runs it to invite the person. Once they've joined, you can share projects with them yourself.

Leave or hand over a project#

  • Leave: in the Share dialog, select Leave next to your own name. The project disappears from your devices; everyone else keeps it.
  • Make owner: the owner can hand the project to another member. The previous owner becomes an admin. Owners can't leave until they've done this.

When someone leaves or is removed, tasks assigned to them become unassigned.

Assign tasks#

In a shared project, each task can be assigned to one member. Open the task and choose someone under Assignee, or select the task and press Shift+A, type a name and press Enter. The assignee's avatar shows on the row, and they get a notification.

Assigned to me in the sidebar (g a) lists every open task assigned to you, across projects.

Comment on a task#

Open a task and scroll to Comments, or press Shift+C with the task open. Write your comment and post it with Comment or Ctrl+Enter (⌘+Enter on a Mac).

  • Mention someone by typing @ and picking their name. They get a notification.
  • Reply to a comment to keep a conversation together. Replies are nested under it.
  • Edit or Delete your own comments. Edited comments are marked as edited. Project admins and the owner can delete any comment.
  • Comments support simple formatting: **bold**, *italic*, `code`, lists, quotes and links.

Everyone who can see a task can comment on it, viewers included. Rows with comments show a speech bubble and a count. Comments work offline too and are sent when you're back online.

The same thread shows the task's activity: who created it, completed it or changed its date.

See what others changed#

Activity in the sidebar (g h) lists the latest changes in all your shared projects, newest first and grouped by day. Each shared project shows a count of unread changes next to its name, and opening the feed marks them as seen. Filter by project, person or kind of change (completed, created, commented, assigned, rescheduled).

Inside a project, Activity at the top (Shift+H) shows the changes for that project only.

Things to know#

  • Labels and reminders stay personal. Labels you add to a shared task are only visible to you, and so are your reminders.
  • Moving a task out of a shared project to your own project or Inbox makes a copy there and removes the original from the shared project for everyone.
  • Deleting a shared project is something only the owner can do. It disappears for every member, and its open tasks are copied into the owner's Inbox.
  • End-to-end encryption and sharing don't mix. Shared projects are never encrypted, and an account with encryption turned on can't share new projects.

pages.title: Notifications
pages.summary: The bell for assignments and mentions, reminder pop-ups inside the app, and push notifications on each device when the app is closed.

toc.text: Get reminders when the app is closed

pages.html:
Notifications

OpenTodo tells you about three things: a task someone assigned to you, a comment that mentions you, and reminders you set. Nothing else, and never anything from outside your server.

The bell#

The bell at the top right shows a red count when something new arrived from other people:

  • assigned you: someone assigned you a task in a shared project,
  • mentioned you: someone wrote @your name in a comment.

Select an entry to open the task. Opening the task marks it as read. You don't get notified about your own actions.

Reminders inside the app#

While OpenTodo is open, a reminder appears in the corner of the screen when it's due, with Snooze 10 min, 1 hour, Tomorrow 09:00 and Dismiss. It needs no permission and no connection. Press Esc to dismiss it.

If the OpenTodo tab is in the background and your browser allows notifications for it, you get a system notification instead.

How to add reminders is covered in Recurring tasks and reminders.

Get reminders when the app is closed#

Push notifications deliver reminders even when OpenTodo isn't open. Each device decides for itself.

  1. Open Settings → Notifications on the device.
  2. Tick Enable notifications on this device and allow notifications when the browser asks.
  3. Select Send test notification to check that one arrives.

Repeat this on every device where you want them: your phone, your laptop, your tablet. Turning it off, or signing out, removes that device.

From a push notification you can Snooze 10 min or Dismiss, and that applies on all your devices.

On iPhone and iPad#

Push needs iOS or iPadOS 16.4 or later, and only works in the installed app. Add OpenTodo to your home screen first (Installing the app), open it from there, then turn on notifications in its settings.

Privacy#

A push message goes through your browser's push service (run by the browser maker). It contains only an id and a time, encrypted so the push service can't read it. Your device then shows the title from its own copy of the task.

Include task titles puts the title in the encrypted message as well, so the notification can show it even before that device has synced the task. Notes are never sent. If your account uses end-to-end encryption, titles are never included.

When notifications don't arrive#

  • "Notifications are blocked for this site": you said no when the browser asked. Allow notifications for your OpenTodo address in the browser's site settings, then select Re-enable.
  • "Push notifications are turned off on this server": the person running your server has switched push off. Reminders still show inside the app.
  • "This browser does not support push notifications": try the installed app, or open OpenTodo over https://.
  • Nothing arrives on a phone: check that the operating system allows notifications for the app (or the browser), and that battery saving or focus modes aren't holding them back.

More fixes in Troubleshooting.

pages.title: Offline and sync
pages.summary: How OpenTodo keeps working without a connection, what the sync status means, and what happens when two devices change the same task.

toc.text: When two devices change the same task

pages.html:
Offline and sync

OpenTodo keeps a full copy of your tasks on each device. Everything you do happens on that copy first, so the app is fast and works the same with or without a connection. Your server keeps every device up to date and holds the backup.

Working offline#

On a train, on a plane, or in a basement with no signal, you can keep going: add tasks, complete them, edit notes, move cards on a board, comment. Your changes wait on the device and are sent as soon as there's a connection again. You don't have to do anything.

The installed app even starts without a connection. See Installing the app.

A few things need the server and say so when you're offline: changing your password, setting up passkeys or two-factor authentication, inviting people, importing files, and the full history of a task.

The sync status#

The status at the top right of the app tells you where things stand.

Status Means
Synced Everything on this device is on the server, and the other way round
Syncing… Sending or receiving changes right now
3 pending Changes are waiting to be sent; they'll go in a moment
Offline · 3 pending No connection; 3 changes will be sent when it's back
Sync error The server answered with a problem; hover over the status for details
Signed out Your session ended; sign in again and waiting changes are sent
Locked Your account uses encryption and this device needs your passphrase

The count is the number of individual changes, not tasks: adding one task with a date and a label counts as several.

Live next to the status means this device gets other devices' changes within seconds. Without it, the app still checks regularly, just less often. Click the status at any time to sync now.

Several devices#

Use OpenTodo on as many devices as you like. A task you add on your phone appears on your laptop within a few seconds when both are online. A device that was off catches up the next time it opens.

When two devices change the same task#

You don't need to resolve conflicts. OpenTodo keeps track of each field of a task separately: the title, the date, the priority, and so on.

  • If your phone changes the date and your laptop changes the priority, both changes are kept.
  • If both change the same field, the change made last wins on every device.
  • Notes are merged: if you type in the same note on two devices, both sets of edits end up in it.
  • If one device deletes a task while another edits it, the task stays deleted. You can restore it from the Trash, edits included.

The same rules apply to people working together in a shared project.

Signing out#

Signing out (Settings → Session → Sign out) removes your tasks from that device. If you're online, waiting changes are sent first. Your data stays on the server, and signing in again downloads it.

Tips#

  • On a shared computer, sign out when you're done.
  • If a device has been offline for weeks, give it a minute after reconnecting to catch up before you start reorganising.
  • Your data lives on your server, and you can download all of it at any time. See Import and export.
  • How sync works under the hood is described in the sync protocol, for the curious.

pages.title: Keyboard shortcuts
pages.summary: Every shortcut in OpenTodo, from quick add to the calendar, plus the optional Vim keybindings.
pages.html:
Keyboard shortcuts

Everything in OpenTodo can be done from the keyboard. You don't need to learn it all: q to add, j / k to move, c to complete and ? to look up the rest gets you a long way.

Shortcuts don't fire while you're typing in a field. Press Esc to leave the field first.

See them in the app#

Press ? at any time for the full list. It's the same list as on this page, generated from the same source, so the two always match.

The ones to learn first#

Keys Does
q Add a task
j / k Move down and up the list
Enter Open the selected task
c Complete it
1 … 4 Set its priority
g then t Go to Today (i for Inbox, u for Upcoming)
Esc Close the panel

A two-step shortcut like g then t means: press g, let go, then press t.

On a Mac, use ⌘ where this page says Ctrl, and Option for Alt.

All shortcuts#

Everywhere#

Keys What it does
q Quick add a task
Shift+V Dictate into quick add (turn voice capture on in Settings first); Esc or a pause stops, Enter saves
Esc Close panel, clear selection
? Toggle this help

Go to a view#

Keys What it does
g then i / t / u / c / l / f / v / s Go to Inbox / Today / Upcoming / Completed / Labels / Filter / Views / Settings
g then a Go to Assigned to me
g then x Go to the Trash
g then h Go to Activity: what changed in your shared projects (j / k select, Enter opens the task, Tab reaches the filters)
g then Shift+I Go to Settings → Import data
g then d / w Go to the Day / Week calendar
g then ? Open Help: the user guide, offline, with search

Tasks in a list#

Keys What it does
j / k Move selection down / up
Enter Open selected task; accept "complete parent too?"
c Complete / reopen selected task (and its subtasks)
a Add a subtask to the selected task
Shift+A Assign the selected task (type to find a member, Enter assigns)
Tab / Shift+Tab Indent under previous sibling / outdent
Alt+↑ / Alt+↓ Move the selected task, or the focused sidebar project, one place within its list (it stays selected)
Alt+Shift+↑ / Alt+Shift+↓ Move it to the top / bottom of its list
Drag (touch: press and hold) Reorder tasks in project lists, boards and the Inbox, and projects in the sidebar; drop on the middle of a row to nest it; Esc cancels
Today, Upcoming, Assigned, Completed, labels, filters Sorted by date (or their own rule): no drag or Alt moves there
← / → Collapse / expand subtasks of the selected task, or sub-projects of the focused sidebar project
v Toggle the current project between list and board (remembered per project on this device)
Shift+S Share the current project: add members by email, change roles, remove, leave, transfer
1 – 4 Set priority of selected task
L Labels of selected task (type to find, Enter adds or creates)
e Edit the estimate of the selected task (type 20, 45m, 1h30; Enter)
s Schedule the selected task: Day view in placement mode
Shift+S Skip the current occurrence of a recurring task
Shift+O Recurring task: this occurrence only (standalone copy, series moves on)
Delete Delete selected task (and its subtasks)
z Task panel open: fix a timed due to your time zone, or release it to a floating time

Board#

Keys What it does
h / l, ← / → Select the first task of the previous / next column; j / k move within a column
Shift+← / Shift+→ Move the selected task to the previous / next column (it stays selected)
a Add a task to the selected task’s column

Day and Week calendar#

Keys What it does
j / k Select the next / previous task (lane, then blocks)
↑ / ↓ Move the selected task 15 minutes (a lane task gets a time)
← / → Move the selected task one day
Shift+↑ / Shift+↓ Shorten / lengthen the estimate by 15 minutes
u / p Unschedule (keep the date) / placement mode for the selected task
Enter / Esc Place the task at the ghost / cancel without changes
[ / ] / t Previous / next day or week, back to today

Filter, saved views and dashboards#

Keys What it does
Enter / Esc In Filter: jump from the query to the first result / back to the query
s In Filter results: save the query as a view, pinned to the sidebar
/ In a saved view: edit the query; Enter saves it, Esc discards
Tab / Shift+Tab On a dashboard: move between panels; j / k inside a panel, Enter opens, o opens the view
↑ / ↓ In the filter query: recall recent queries on this device

Trash and projects#

Keys What it does
m Move the current project under another project or to the top level
j / k, r, Delete In the Trash: select, restore, delete permanently (Enter confirms, Esc cancels)
Enter After completing the last task of a project: archive the project; any other key dismisses

Comments and notes#

Keys What it does
Shift+C Comment on the open task: focus the composer (markdown; @ completes members, ↑ / ↓ and Enter pick)
Ctrl+Enter / ⌘+Enter In a comment: post the comment, reply or edit; Esc cancels or leaves the field
Tab, Enter In the comment thread: reach Reply, Edit and Delete on a comment; Load older activity at the end
Shift+H In a project: show or hide the project activity; Tab reaches the person and kind filters
Ctrl/⌘+B, I, Shift+X, E, K In the notes: bold, italic, strikethrough, inline code, link
Ctrl/⌘+Alt+1–3 / 0 In the notes: heading 1–3 / normal text
Ctrl/⌘+Shift+8 / 7 / 9 In the notes: bullet, numbered, check list; Ctrl/⌘+Enter ticks a check item; Tab / Shift+Tab indent
- · 1. · # · [ ] · x Typed in the notes: markdown typing becomes formatting; Shift+Enter is a line break, Esc leaves the notes

Settings#

Keys What it does
Enter On an invitation: Settings → Members: copy the invite link created in this session
Delete On an invitation: Settings → Members: revoke a pending invitation
d / r / Delete On a user: Settings → Users: deactivate or reactivate, create a reset link, delete (each confirms)
g then s, Tab Settings → Security: add, rename (Enter saves, Esc cancels) or delete passkeys

Quick add syntax#

Type What it does
<code>tomorrow · next Wed · 3 Feb · at 3pm</code> Due date and time (6 languages)
<code>#project @label p1 +30m</code> Project, label, priority, estimate
<code>"quoted text"</code> Keep text literally
Backspace ×2 End of line: highlight, then dismiss the last chip

Vim keybindings#

If you're used to Vim, turn on Settings → Keyboard → Vim keybindings. It's off by default and applies to that device only. With it on, a small indicator shows the mode (Normal, Insert or Command), and you get:

  • counts like 3j, gg and G for the first and last task,
  • dd to delete, x to complete, o to add a task below and i to edit,
  • J / K to move the selected task,
  • a command line on : with :today, :project <name>, :new <title>, :sync and :help.

All the usual shortcuts keep working. With Vim keybindings on, the ? list includes a Vim section.

pages.title: Account security
pages.summary: Sign in with a passkey, add two-factor authentication, change your password and check where your account is signed in.
pages.html:
Account security

Your password is the starting point. A passkey makes signing in quicker and safer, and two-factor authentication adds a second lock. All of it lives in Settings, and none of it involves anyone outside your server.

These settings need a connection to your server. While you're offline they're shown read-only.

Sign in with a passkey#

A passkey lets you sign in with your fingerprint, face or device PIN instead of typing a password. It can't be phished or reused on another site, and your password keeps working as a fallback.

  1. Open Settings → Security.
  2. Select Add passkey and give it a name you'll recognise, like "Work laptop".
  3. Confirm with your fingerprint, face or PIN when your device asks.

Next time, choose Sign in with a passkey on the sign-in screen, or pick it from the suggestions in the email field.

Add a passkey on a second device too, so losing one isn't a problem. You can rename or delete passkeys in the same list. If one is marked as suspicious, OpenTodo noticed something that looks like a copied passkey; delete it if you don't recognise the device.

If you don't see the Security section, passkeys aren't available on your server. They need a secure https:// address; ask whoever runs your server.

Turn on two-factor authentication#

With two-factor authentication, signing in takes your password plus a six-digit code from an authenticator app on your phone. Any app that supports time-based codes works.

  1. Open Settings → Two-factor authentication and select Set up two-factor authentication.
  2. Scan the QR code with your authenticator app, or type in the key shown under it.
  3. Enter the six-digit code the app shows.
  4. Save the recovery codes that appear. They're shown only once: download them as a text file or write them down and keep them somewhere safe.

From then on, sign-in asks for a code after your password. Signing in with a passkey skips the code, because the passkey already checks it's you.

Remember this browser#

When you enter a code, you can tick Remember this device for 30 days so that browser doesn't ask again for a month. The list of remembered browsers is under Two-factor authentication, where you can forget them.

Recovery codes#

Each recovery code works once, in place of a code from the app. Use one if you lose your phone. Settings shows how many you have left and lets you generate a new set, which replaces the old one.

If you lose both your phone and your recovery codes, the owner of your server can reset your two-factor authentication.

Your server's owner can also make two-factor authentication required. If so, you'll be asked to set it up when you sign in, and you can't turn it off.

Change your password#

Open Settings → Password, enter your current password and a new one of at least 10 characters. Changing it signs you out everywhere else; the device you're on stays signed in.

Forgot it? There's no self-service reset by email. Ask the owner or an admin of your server for a reset link. If you're the owner, see recovering owner access.

Check recent sign-ins#

Settings → Recent activity lists sign-ins and token changes on your account from the last 90 days. If you see one you don't recognise, change your password, revoke your API tokens and tell the owner of your server.

Confirm it's you#

Some changes, like creating an API token or turning off two-factor authentication, ask for your password or a code again, unless you entered one in the last ten minutes. That keeps someone who finds your unlocked laptop from changing them.

Sign out#

Settings → Session → Sign out ends your session on that device and removes your tasks from it. Changes that haven't been sent yet are uploaded first when you're online.

More protection#

  • End-to-end encryption encrypts your task titles, notes and comments on your devices, so even your server only stores scrambled text.
  • If your server uses a company or family login (single sign-on), you can link it under Settings → Linked accounts and sign in with it.

pages.title: Import and export
pages.summary: Download everything you have as one file, and bring tasks in from a spreadsheet, another OpenTodo server or other task apps.
pages.html:
Import and export

Your tasks are yours. You can download all of them at any time, and bring tasks in from other places. Nothing is locked in.

Download everything#

Open Settings → Your data and select Download export (JSON). You get one file with all your projects, sections, tasks and subtasks, labels, reminders and saved views, including completed tasks and items in the Trash. Shared projects you're a member of are included too.

The file is plain JSON, so you can open it in any text editor, keep it as a backup, or load it into another OpenTodo server.

The person who runs your server can also set up automatic backups of the whole server.

Import from another app#

Open Settings → Import data (or press g then Shift+I) and choose a file. OpenTodo accepts:

  • an OpenTodo export, for moving to another server or restoring,
  • a CSV file, from a spreadsheet or a script, with a title column and optional columns for project, due date, priority, labels and more,
  • JSON exports from other task apps, in the common shapes those apps use.

Nothing is written straight away. OpenTodo first shows a preview:

  1. Check the format it detected. You can change it if it guessed wrong.
  2. Choose the options: which project gets tasks that have none, the time zone for dates, whether sections stay sections or become labels, and what to do with possible duplicates and with rows that have errors.
  3. Read the preview table. Each row says what will happen: created, updated, skipped (with the reason) or an error (with the reason). Problems are listed first.
  4. Import. The import runs on the server, and the tasks reach all your devices on their next sync.

Recurring rules, reminders, subtasks, sections and completed tasks come across where the file has them. Anything OpenTodo can't store is listed as a warning on its row, never dropped silently.

Duplicates#

Importing the same file twice won't double your tasks. OpenTodo recognises rows it imported before, and flags tasks that look like ones you already have (same title, project and due date). Those are skipped unless you choose Import them anyway.

For an OpenTodo export, items that already exist on the server are kept as they are, unless you choose to overwrite changed fields.

Undo an import#

Every import appears under Past imports, with a summary. Undo removes everything that import created and leaves the rest alone. Tasks you added later to an imported project move to your Inbox rather than disappearing. You can then import the same file again, for example with different options.

Good to know#

  • Import needs a connection to your server.
  • Files can be up to 20 MB and 50,000 rows, unless your server allows more.
  • Comments aren't imported. The preview tells you how many there were.
  • In a CSV file, write dates as 2026-10-15 and put a time like 09:30 in a due_time column. The import reference lists every column, with an example file.
  • If a JSON export from another app isn't recognised, convert it to CSV. Every field OpenTodo stores can be written as a CSV column.

The import formats reference has the details: each format, how fields are mapped, recurring rules and reminders.

pages.title: Trash and history
pages.summary: Restore deleted tasks and projects from the Trash, see every change made to a task, and bring back an earlier value.

toc.text: See what changed on a task

pages.html:
Trash and history

Deleting something in OpenTodo doesn't make it vanish. It goes to the Trash first, and every change to a task is kept in its history, so a slip of the finger is easy to undo.

Restore something from the Trash#

Open Trash in the sidebar (or press g x). It lists deleted tasks and projects, newest first, with when they were deleted and how many days they have left.

Select Restore next to an item. It comes back exactly where it was:

  • A restored project returns to its place in the sidebar, with all its tasks.
  • A restored task returns to its project. If that project is still in the Trash, the task goes to your Inbox instead.

With the keyboard: j / k to select, r to restore.

Delete for good#

Delete permanently removes one item for good, and Empty Trash removes everything in it. Both ask you to confirm, and both need a connection. Once something is permanently deleted, it's gone from every device and from the server, and it can't come back.

Items are also deleted for good automatically after 30 days in the Trash. Your server's owner can change that period or turn it off.

What deleting does#

  • Deleting a task also deletes its subtasks.
  • Deleting a project hides it and its tasks everywhere. Its sub-projects move up a level, so they aren't lost.
  • Reminders on deleted tasks stay quiet. Restore the task and they work again.
  • Deleted items are still in your export until they are deleted for good.

See what changed on a task#

Open a task and select History at the bottom of its panel. You see every change, newest first: what the field was, what it became, when, and from where (this device, another device, the API, a calendar app, or an AI assistant). Changes made by an AI assistant read "AI assistant (token name)" for your own assistants and "AI assistant" for someone else's in a shared project, and can be restored like any other change.

Projects have a History too, at the top of the project.

History is loaded from your server, so it needs a connection.

Bring back an earlier value#

Next to each change in the history is Restore this value. Select it to set the field back to what it was then. Restoring is a change like any other: it syncs to all devices and shows up in the history itself, so you can always undo the undo.

Activity on a task#

The comment thread of a task also shows its activity: who created it, completed it, moved it or changed the date. In shared projects this includes everyone's changes. See Sharing and comments.

Archived projects#

Archiving is different from deleting. An archived project disappears from the sidebar, but it isn't in the Trash and isn't deleted after 30 days: it and its tasks are kept as they are. Archive a project from its Project menu.

When you complete the last task of a project, OpenTodo offers to archive it. Projects without open tasks for 30 days are archived automatically, with a notice that has an undo button. To switch automatic archiving off on a device, untick the option under Settings → Projects.

Bring back an archived project#

Open Settings → Projects. Under Archived projects you see every archived project, with its parent project and how many open tasks it has. Select Restore next to one, and it's back in the sidebar with all its tasks. With the keyboard, Tab to the button and press Enter.

  • Restoring works offline, like any change, and the project comes back on your other devices after they sync.
  • Restoring brings back that one project. If you archived a project with sub-projects, they stay in the list until you restore each of them.
  • A project you restore by hand isn't archived automatically again on that device.
  • In a shared project, only the owner or an admin can restore it, the same people who can archive it.

pages.title: Settings
pages.summary: A tour of Settings, what each section does, which choices belong to one device and which follow your account.

toc.text: How the app behaves on this device

pages.html:
Settings

Open Settings with the gear next to your name at the bottom of the sidebar, or press g then s. It's one long page. This guide walks through it from top to bottom.

Some settings follow your account to every device. Others belong to the device you're on, so your phone and laptop can be set up differently. Settings that apply to one device say "this device" next to them.

Each section has a Help link on the right that opens its part of this guide next to Settings.

What you see depends on your role: people who run the server see extra sections, and the public demo hides most account and server settings.

Your data#

Download export (JSON) saves everything you have in one file. Import data… brings in tasks from a file. See Import and export.

Calendar#

When the Day and Week grid starts and ends, and how long your working day is. Each device keeps its own. See Time blocking.

Your account#

  • Password: change your password. See Account security.
  • Two-factor authentication: a code from your phone on top of your password. See Account security.
  • End-to-end encryption: encrypt your task text on your devices. See End-to-end encryption.
  • Notifications: push notifications for reminders on this device. See Notifications.
  • Security: passkeys. See Account security.
  • Linked accounts: connect a single sign-on login, if your server offers one.
  • Recent activity: sign-ins and token changes from the last 90 days.
  • Session: Sign out of this device. This also removes your tasks from it; changes not yet sent are uploaded first.

How the app behaves on this device#

  • Start view: the view this device opens on. See Views.
  • Keyboard: turn on Vim keybindings. See Keyboard shortcuts.
  • Projects: archive projects automatically after 30 days without open tasks, and bring back archived projects with Restore. See Trash and history.
  • Quick add: turn natural-language parsing on or off, pick the languages it understands, and the order of day and month in dates like 12/11. See Quick add syntax.
  • Voice capture: dictate tasks into quick add. Off until you turn it on, and the app explains first what your browser does with the audio. See Quick add syntax.
  • Capture: the Add to OpenTodo bookmarklet, to save the page you're reading as a task. See Capturing pages.

Connect other apps#

These sections connect OpenTodo to other tools. Some appear only when the person running your server has switched the feature on.

  • Calendar apps (CalDAV): see your tasks in calendar and reminder apps on your phone or computer, with an app password. See Calendar apps.
  • Webhooks: send a message to another service when tasks change. See Webhooks.
  • Email to task: your own secret address; emails sent there become tasks. See Email to task.
  • AI assistants: give an AI assistant read-only access to your tasks, or, when the server owner allows it and you switch on Allow AI assistants to make changes, a token for an assistant that can make changes you can undo. See AI assistants (MCP).
  • API tokens: keys for scripts and the ot command-line client. A token is shown once, when you create it. Read-only tokens can't change anything; tokens for an AI assistant that can make changes work only through the assistant tools and never on the rest of the API. See HTTP API and Command-line client.

For server admins#

If you're the owner or an admin of the server, you also see:

  • Members: invite people with a single-use link. See Sharing and comments.
  • Users: everyone with an account, their role and last sign-in. Make someone an admin (owner only), deactivate or reactivate an account, create a password reset link, or delete an account.
  • Single sign-on: sign-in through your company or family identity provider (owner only). See Single sign-on.
  • Backups: scheduled backups to a folder, S3 or WebDAV (owner only). See Backups.
  • The policy under Two-factor authentication: make it optional, required for the owner, or required for everyone (owner only).

Running the server itself is covered in Running with Docker.

pages.title: Troubleshooting and FAQ
pages.summary: Fixes for the usual hiccups, from a task that seems to be missing to reminders that don't arrive, and answers to common questions.

toc.text: A task seems to be missing
Changes don't show up on my other device
The demo says my sandbox expired
I can't install the app or add a passkey
I can't edit a shared project
I can't share a project with someone
The app looks out of date

pages.html:
Troubleshooting and FAQ

Most problems have a quick fix. Start with the section that matches what you see. If nothing here helps, the person who runs your server can look at its logs, or you can open an issue on GitHub.

A task seems to be missing#

Check these places, in this order:

  1. A filter above the list. If Quick wins, Under 30 min, Over 1 h or Unestimated is switched on, the list shows only matching tasks. Select it again to clear it.
  2. Completed. It may have been ticked off by accident. Open Completed and reopen it.
  3. Trash. It may have been deleted, or its project was. See Trash and history.
  4. An archived project. Tasks of archived projects don't appear in Today or Upcoming.
  5. A folded parent or section. Select the small arrow to unfold it.
  6. A shared project you left or were removed from. Ask its owner.

The Filter view with search: word (add & completed to include finished tasks) searches titles and notes.

Changes don't show up on my other device#

  • Look at the status at the top right of both devices. Offline · 3 pending means the changes are still waiting on that device; they're sent as soon as it's online.
  • Click the status to sync right away.
  • Sync error: hover over it to see the reason. If the server is down or being updated, it clears up once the server is back.
  • Signed out: your session ended. Sign in again; waiting changes are sent afterwards.
  • Locked: your account uses encryption. Enter your passphrase on that device.

See Offline and sync for what each status means.

I can't sign in#

  • Check the email address and that Caps Lock is off. Passwords are at least 10 characters.
  • After several failed attempts, the server makes you wait a little before trying again.
  • Forgot your password? OpenTodo doesn't send reset emails. Ask the owner or an admin of your server for a reset link. If you are the owner, see recovering owner access.
  • Lost your two-factor phone? Use one of your recovery codes instead of the code. Without them, the server owner can reset your two-factor authentication.

The demo says my sandbox expired#

Demo sandboxes are deleted after two hours without activity, after 24 hours at most, and every night. Select Start a new sandbox to get a fresh one. Nothing from the old sandbox is kept.

Reminders don't arrive#

Inside the app, reminders pop up while it's open. To get them when the app is closed, push notifications must be turned on for each device in Settings → Notifications, and on an iPhone only the installed app can receive them. Notifications lists the messages you might see and what to do.

I can't install the app or add a passkey#

Both need your server to be on a secure https:// address. If the browser offers no install option, or Settings has no Security section for passkeys, ask whoever runs your server. Instructions per device are in Installing the app.

Quick add got it wrong#

If a word was read as a date, project or priority by mistake, select the × on its chip before you press Enter, or press Backspace twice at the end of the line. Text in double quotes is never interpreted: Read "Next Friday". You can also switch parsing off in Settings → Quick add. See Quick add syntax.

I can't edit a shared project#

Your role in that project is viewer, which is read-only. Ask the owner or an admin to make you an editor. See Sharing and comments.

I can't share a project with someone#

You can only add people who have an account on your server. Ask an admin of the server to invite them first. Accounts with end-to-end encryption turned on can't share new projects.

The app looks out of date#

The app updates itself when your server is updated. If something still looks old, close it completely (all tabs or the installed window) and open it again.

Something went wrong on screen#

If a part of the app fails to display, you see a message with a Reload button. Your tasks are stored on the device and aren't lost by reloading.

Frequently asked questions#

Does OpenTodo work without internet?#

Yes. Each device keeps a full copy of your tasks, and changes are sent when you're back online. See Offline and sync.

Where are my tasks stored?#

On your devices and on the OpenTodo server you use. Nothing goes to anyone else: the app has no tracking and no analytics, and it only talks to your own server.

Is there an app in the app stores?#

No. OpenTodo is a web app that you install from your server's address, and it then behaves like any other app. See Installing the app.

Can I use OpenTodo on my own, without a server?#

OpenTodo needs a server to sign in and sync, but it can be small: a single container on a Raspberry Pi or a cheap virtual server is enough. To try it first, use the demo. Setting up a server is described in Running with Docker.

Can I move my tasks from another task app?#

Usually, yes. OpenTodo imports CSV files and the JSON exports of other task apps. See Import and export.

Can several people use one server?#

Yes. The owner invites people, each person has their own account and private tasks, and projects can be shared between them. See Sharing and comments.

What does it cost?#

Nothing. OpenTodo is free software under the AGPL-3.0 licence. There's no subscription and no paid tier.

pages.title: Quick add syntax
pages.summary: Every word quick add understands: dates, times, projects, labels, priorities, estimates, six languages and voice capture.
pages.html:
Quick add syntax

Type one line in the quick-add box (press q in any task view) and OpenTodo picks out the due date and time, project, labels, priority and estimate:

Meeting with Sarah next Wed at 3pm #work @call p1 +30m

creates Meeting with Sarah, due next Wednesday at 15:00, in project Work, with the label call, priority 1, estimated at 30 minutes.

Everything runs in your browser. The parser needs no network, sends nothing anywhere, and gives the same result on every device for the same line, date, languages and projects. The created task stores the resolved date, so other devices never parse the line again.

Preview chips#

As you type, each thing OpenTodo recognises shows up as a chip under the input, and the title preview (→ Meeting with Sarah) shows what will be saved. Nothing is hidden: if there is no chip, the text stays in the title.

To… Do this
Keep a word literally ("may" is not May 1st) Click the × on its chip, or press Backspace at the end of the line: the first press highlights the last chip, the second dismisses it. The text itself is not changed.
Never parse some text Put it in double quotes: Watch "Next Friday" tomorrow → title Watch Next Friday, due tomorrow. The quotes are removed from the title.
Turn parsing off on this device Settings → Quick add → Parse natural language in quick add. Quick add then saves the line exactly as typed.

A dismissed chip stays dismissed while you keep typing; it comes back only if you edit that word. Backspace only highlights a chip when that chip's text ends the line; otherwise Backspace deletes text as usual.

Tokens (any language)#

Token Meaning Examples
#name Project, including sub-projects at any depth. Case-insensitive; spaces, - and _ in project names are ignored. An exact name wins, otherwise a unique prefix. If several projects have exactly that name (say Docs under both Work and Home), the shallowest one in the tree wins (a fixed tie-break by id decides between equals, so every device picks the same one); the chip shows the path (#Work › Docs) so you can see which. Archived and deleted projects are skipped. If nothing matches, or a prefix fits more than one project, the token stays in the title. #work, #trav (Travel), #sideproject (Side Project), #q4 (Work › Docs › Q4 launch)
@name Label, matched to an existing label ignoring case. A name with no label yet creates one when you press Enter, with the next free colour, exactly like creating it from the label picker; its chip says new until then. Use as many as you like. @call, @waiting-for
p1–p4 Priority, 1 highest, 4 default. p1, P3
+duration Estimate in minutes, from 1 minute to 7 days (10080 minutes). Shown on the task row. +30, +30m, +45min, +2h, +1h30, +1.5h

Without the +, 45min and 2h also work, except that 2h is left alone when French, Spanish or Portuguese is active, because those languages write times as 15h.

Dates and times#

Phrase Resolves to
today, tonight, tomorrow, day after tomorrow that day
Monday … Sunday, mon, wed. the next one after today (on a Friday, fri means next Friday)
this sat same as the bare weekday
next Monday same as the bare weekday, unless that day is still in the current Monday–Sunday week; then the one a week later. On Friday 9 Oct, next Wed is 14 Oct and next Sat is 17 Oct (not tomorrow).
in 3 days, in 2 weeks, in a month today plus that much (months keep the day, clamped to the month's end)
next week, next month Monday of next week; the 1st of next month
3 Feb, Feb 3, 3rd of February, December 25th 2027 that date; without a year, the next time it comes round (today counts)
May, December (full name alone) the 1st of that month. Abbreviations (mar, jan) need a day number next to them.
12/11, 12-11, 12/11/2027, 2026-11-03 numeric dates; see day/month order below
at 3pm, 3:30 pm, 16:30, at 9, noon, midnight that time today, unless a date is also given. A time on its own always means today, even if it has passed. Without am/pm, hours are 24-hour (at 3 is 03:00).
in 3 hours that clock time, rolling to tomorrow past midnight

Words like on, by and due in front of a date are removed with it (Pay bill by Friday → Pay bill). Bare numbers are never times (Buy 3 apples stays as typed): write at 3, 3pm or 15:00.

When a line has two dates, the first one counts and the second stays in the title. The same goes for a second time, project, priority or estimate.

Day/month order. 12/11 is 11 December when your first language is US English (en, en-US) and 12 November for every other language, including English outside the US. If one reading is impossible (25/12), the other is used. Dotted dates (12.11.) are always day.month and only used when the order is day/month. Change it under Settings → Quick add.

Languages#

Vocabulary is bundled for English, German, French, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese. The active languages are your browser's preferred languages that are bundled, plus English, which is always on; all of them are matched at the same time. Settings → Quick add can override the list on this device. Where two languages read a word differently, the longer phrase wins (Spanish mar alone is Tuesday; mar 3 is March 3rd).

Examples
German heute, morgen, übermorgen, am Freitag, Mi., nächsten Mittwoch um 15 Uhr, in 3 Tagen, nächste Woche, 3. Februar, 12.11., 14:30 Uhr
French aujourd'hui, demain à 15h, après-demain, mardi prochain, dans 2 semaines, semaine prochaine, 3 février, 15h30, à 9 heures, midi
Italian oggi, domani alle 15, dopodomani, lunedì prossimo, prossimo sabato, tra 3 giorni, fra una settimana, il 3 febbraio, mezzogiorno
Spanish hoy, mañana a las 15:00, pasado mañana, el próximo lunes, martes que viene, en 3 días, dentro de 2 semanas, 3 de febrero
Portuguese hoje, amanhã às 15h, depois de amanhã, próxima segunda, sábado que vem, daqui a 3 dias, em 2 semanas, 3 de fevereiro

Accents are optional (manana, nachsten, fevrier work too). Two-letter German abbreviations need their dot (Mi., Do.) so ordinary words like do and so are not mistaken for weekdays.

Views and defaults#

Quick add still takes the view's context for anything the line does not set: today in Today, tomorrow in Upcoming, the current project in a project view, the current label in a label view. Anything the line does set wins, so Plan trip next Monday #travel typed in Today goes to Travel on Monday. Labels add up instead: @call typed in the errand label view gives the task both labels, so it stays in the view you added it from.

Voice#

Quick add can also be dictated. Voice capture is off by default and is switched on per device in Settings → Voice capture; it is not synced, so turning it on for your phone leaves your laptop as it is. Browsers without speech recognition (Firefox, for example) show the switch disabled with an explanation, and quick add has no microphone button there.

With voice capture on, press the microphone button in quick add or Shift+V anywhere outside a text field (plain v already toggles list and board in a project). Words appear in the box as they are recognised; when you stop talking, press the button again or press Esc, the final transcript is inserted at the caret and parsed exactly like typed text, chips included. Nothing is saved until you press Enter, so you can correct the line by hand first.

Spoken forms of the tokens are turned into their typed forms first, in the active quick-add languages (English is always on):

Said Becomes
"renew insurance hashtag home priority two" renew insurance #home p2
"standup at nine thirty am" standup at 9:30am
"call the dentist tomorrow at nine" call the dentist tomorrow at 9
"label errands buy stamps" @errands buy stamps
"phone mum at call" (an existing label call) phone mum @call
"plan move project home office" (an existing project) plan move #homeoffice
"write report for thirty minutes", "one hour and fifteen minutes" write report +30m, +75m
"ping Ana in two hours" ping Ana in 2 hours
"um neun Uhr dreißig", "alle nove", "a las diez", "à neuf heures", "às onze" um 9:30, alle 9, a las 10, à 9 heures, às 11

Trigger words per language: hashtag (all), project / Projekt / projet / progetto / proyecto / projeto (only before an existing project's name), label / Etikett / étiquette / etichetta / etiqueta, and priority / Priorität / priorité / priorità / prioridad / prioridade followed by one to four. Numbers are only converted next to a time, priority or duration cue, so "buy two apples" stays as it is.
